1.pericope_label: Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned thirty and one years in Jerusalem. And his mother’s name was Jedidah, the daughter of Adaiah of Boscath. And he did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, and walked in all the way of David his father, and turned not aside to the right hand or to the left. And it came to pass in the eighteenth year of king Josiah, that the king sent Shaphan the son of Azaliah, the son of Meshullam, the scribe, to the house of the Lord, saying, Go up to Hilkiah the high priest, that he may sum the silver which is brought into the house of the Lord, which the keepers of the door have gathered of the people: And let them deliver it into the hand of the doers of the work, that have the oversight of the house of the Lord: and let them give it to the doers of the work which is in the house of the Lord, to repair the breaches of the house, Unto carpenters, and builders, and masons, and to buy timber and hewn stone to repair the house. Howbeit there was no reckoning made with them of the money that was delivered into their hand, because they dealt faithfully. And Hilkiah the high priest said unto Shaphan the scribe, I have found the book of the law in the house of the Lord. And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan, and he read it. And Shaphan the scribe came to the king, and brought the king word again, and said, Thy servants have gathered the money that was found in the house, and have delivered it into the hand of them that do the work, that have the oversight of the house of the Lord. And Shaphan the scribe shewed the king, saying, Hilkiah the priest hath delivered me a book. And Shaphan read it before the king.

schools.summary: Ellicott begins with the name, which seems to mean that Jah heals, and places Boscath in the lowland of Judah; the eight-year-old accession he takes to mean that the queen-mother was probably paramount in the government during the first years of the reign, and the thirty-one years he reckons at somewhat over, on the evidence of the prophetic datings, by which it was twenty-three years from the thirteenth of Josiah to the fourth of Jehoiakim. On the eighteenth year he answers a critic who had called the discourses of Jeremiah, who began his prophetic ministry in the thirteenth year, incomprehensible on the assumption that idolatry was extirpated throughout the country in the twelfth: the discourses would be reconcilable even with that assumption, which however it is not necessary to make, since Josiah did not succeed, any more than Hezekiah, in rooting out the spirit of apostasy. He notes that the young king was no doubt influenced for good by the discourses of Jeremiah and Zephaniah, and reports the difficulty of accounting for his heeding the prophetic teachings at all, considering that as the grandson of a Manasseh and the son of an Amon he must have been brought up under precisely opposite influences. On the embassy he defends the fuller list given in Chronicles against a critic who pronounced the additional personages fictitious, taking the four grounds one by one and answering each, and reserving his sharpest reply for the argument from a repeated name, as if anything could be inferred from the recurrence of the same name, and that probably in the same family. The grammar of the clause about the reckoning he settles by making it part of the royal mandate, only let there be no reckoning, and notes that the same construction is used elsewhere in this book in a different sense. On the finding he works from the form of the words: it is literally the book of the Torah that the high priest says he has found, and the definite form of the expression proves that what he found was something already known, not a book but the book of the Law. He then reports how little the critics are agreed as to its precise character and contents, the whole then existing Scripture, the five books, the ordered collection of Mosaic laws in the middle three, the second book and the fifth having each been proposed and each rejected on the ground that all of them must have been brought into their present shape at a later time; the proposal he reports with approval is that of a collection of the statutes and ordinances of Moses afterwards worked up into the five books and especially into the fifth, called the book of the covenant, already existing in the time of Jehoshaphat, probably preserved in the ark and put on one side in the reign of Manasseh, so that when it was found again after half a century of disuse it appeared like something new because it had been wholly forgotten. On the report brought back to the king he corrects the rendering, that the servants had not gathered but poured out the money from the alms-chest into the bags, and prefers the reading of Chronicles for the place. And on the reading he notes that a critic infers from the single verb that the book was of no great size, and that if it were meant that the whole was read we should expect all the words of the book in the next verse. Delitzsch sets the chapter's structure out first: after a brief account of the length and spirit of the reign there follows a closely connected narrative of what Josiah did for the restoration of worship, and the whole of the reform effected by him is placed in the eighteenth year of his reign because it was in that year that the book of the law was discovered, through which the reformation of worship was carried to completion. It is evident, he says, that it was the historian's intention to combine together everything Josiah did to this end so as to form one grand picture, from the circumstance that he has not merely placed the chronological datum at the beginning but has repeated it at the close. He then marks the long period in the Hebrew, that the clause beginning it came to pass in the eighteenth year has no apodosis until the eighth verse, where Hilkiah speaks; identifies the scribe as the secretary of state; and on the reading observes that the Hebrew verb does not signify that the whole was read, as is evident from the comparison with the next chapter, where the reading of the whole is expressed differently.

Clarke gives the chapter's argument at the head and then praises the king without qualification: he was one of the best, if not the best, of all the Jewish kings since the time of David, and he began well, continued well and ended well. On the summing of the silver he does the arithmetic of the neglect: since Josiah began to seek the Lord as soon as he began to reign, we may naturally conclude that the worship of God neglected and suppressed by his father was immediately restored and the people began their accustomed offerings, so that ten years had elapsed since these offerings began, and no one had as yet taken account of them, nor were they applied to the use for which they were given. On the book he asks directly whether this was the autograph of Moses and thinks it very probable that it was, since the parallel account calls it the book of the law of the Lord by Moses; and he supposes it to be that part of the fifth book which contains the renewing of the covenant in the plains of Moab, and which contains the most terrible invectives against the corrupters of God's word and worship. He reports the rabbinical story that three of the idolatrous kings endeavoured to destroy all the copies of the law, and that this one was saved by having been buried under a paving-stone. But he will not have it that this was the only copy in Judea, and gives four reasons: that even granting the attempt, those kings could not have succeeded so as to destroy the whole; that Manasseh after his conversion endeavoured to restore every part of the divine worship, in which he could have done nothing without the five books; that the succeeding reign of Amon was too short to undo what his penitent father had reformed; and that in the time of Jehoshaphat teaching from the law was universal in the land, that king having set an itinerant ministry on foot in order to instruct the people fully. Wesley agrees with Clarke about what the book was, calling it that original book of the law of the Lord given or written by the hand of Moses, as the parallel account expresses it, which by God's command was put beside the ark, and probably taken from thence and hid by the care of some godly priest when the idolatrous kings of Judah persecuted the true religion and defaced the temple, and, as the Jewish writers affirm, burnt all the copies of God's law they could find; it was now found among the rubbish, or in some secret place. The scribe he glosses briefly as the secretary of state.

Henry takes the young king's case as an argument about grace. Solomon says, woe unto thee O land when thy king is a child, but happy art thou O land when thy king is such a child, and our English Israel once had a king that was such a child. Being young, Josiah had not received any bad impressions from the example of his father and grandfather, but soon saw their errors, and God gave him grace to take warning by them; and Henry presses the sovereignty of that grace, the father passed by and left to perish in his sin while the son is a chosen vessel, and its triumphs, since Josiah was born of a wicked father with no good education nor good example given him, with many about him who no doubt advised him to tread in his father's steps and few that gave him good counsel, and yet the grace of God made him an eminent saint, cutting him off from the wild olive and grafting him into the good. He walked in a good way and turned not aside to the right hand nor to the left, for there are errors on both hands, and he fell neither into superstition nor into profaneness. The eighteenth year Henry explains by resistance rather than arrangement: Josiah began much sooner to seek the Lord, but it is to be feared the work of reformation went slowly on and met with much opposition, so that he could not effect what he desired and designed till his power was thoroughly confirmed; and the consideration of the time we unavoidably lose in our minority should quicken us, when we have come to years, to act with so much the more vigour in the service of God, since having begun late we have need to work hard. On the collection he commends the method, that they took much the same way of raising the money that had been taken in an earlier reign, and that when people gave a little at a time the burden was insensible, and the contribution being voluntary it was not complained of. Over the clause that no reckoning was made with the workmen he divides against himself: it is certainly mentioned to the praise of the workmen, that they gained such a reputation for honesty, but whether to the praise of those that employed them he does not know, for a man should count money after his own father, and it would not have been amiss to have reckoned with the workmen, that others also might be satisfied of their honesty. The finding of the book he treats as a providence. It seems the book was lost or missing, and he offers three accounts of how: that it was carelessly mislaid and neglected, thrown by into a corner as some throw their Bibles, by those who knew not its value; or maliciously concealed by some of the idolatrous kings or their agents, who being restrained from burning it buried it in hopes it would never see the light again; or carefully laid up by some of its friends lest it should fall into the hands of its enemies. Whoever were the instruments of its preservation, he says, we ought to acknowledge the hand of God in it; if this was the only authentic copy of the five books then in being, which had so narrow a turn for its life, he wonders the hearts of all good people did not tremble for that sacred treasure as Eli's did for the ark, and we have reason to thank God upon our knees for the happy providence by which Hilkiah found it when he sought it not. If the holy Scriptures had not been of God they would not have been in being at this day, and God's care of the Bible is a plain indication of his interest in it. For how the things in it could be new to both king and high priest he supposes that neither the command for the king to write out a copy of the law nor that for the public reading of the law every seventh year had been observed for a long time, and that when the instituted means of keeping up religion are neglected religion itself will soon decay. Yet if the book was lost, he grants the difficulty of saying what rule Josiah went by in doing right and how the priests kept up the rites of their religion, and he is apt to think the people generally took up with abstracts of the law, like our abridgements of the statutes, a sort of ritual directing them in their observances but leaving out what the priests thought fit, and particularly the promises and threatenings, which he observes were just the portions that so affected Josiah because they were new to him; no summaries or extracts out of the Bible, he concludes, can be effectual to convey and preserve the knowledge of God and his will like the Bible itself, and it was no marvel the people were so corrupt when the book of the law was such a scarce thing among them. He makes the timing itself a token for good, that the book was brought to light to direct and quicken the reformation already begun, and notes that they were about a good work, repairing the temple, when they found it, since those who do their duty according to their knowledge shall have their knowledge increased; and he hears the high priest's own delight in the words, rejoice with me, for I have found the book of the law, the richest jewel of the king's crown.

debates: What the book of the law was, where Clarke asks whether it was the autograph of Moses and thinks it very probable, supposing it the part of the fifth book containing the renewing of the covenant in the plains of Moab, and Wesley says the same, the original book written by the hand of Moses and put beside the ark, while Henry takes it for the autograph or at least an ancient and authentic copy, most likely the one laid up by Moses' command in the most holy place; against all three Ellicott reasons from the definite form of the expression that what was found was not a book but the book, something already known, and reports the critics in complete disagreement, the whole Scripture, the five books, the middle three, the second and the fifth having each been proposed and rejected, in favour of a collection of Mosaic statutes afterwards worked up into the five books.

Whether this was the only copy of the law in Judea, where Henry entertains the possibility and says that if so he wonders the hearts of all good people did not tremble for that sacred treasure as Eli's did for the ark, and explains how both king and high priest could find its contents new by supposing that the people had till then only abstracts of the law, like abridgements of the statutes, leaving out the promises and threatenings; while Clarke calls the supposition scarcely reasonable and answers it on four grounds, that the idolatrous kings could not have destroyed the whole, that Manasseh after his conversion could not have restored the worship without the five books, that Amon's reign was too short to undo his father's reformation, and that in Jehoshaphat's time teaching from the law was universal by an itinerant ministry.

Why the whole reformation is dated to the eighteenth year, where Delitzsch makes it the historian's deliberate arrangement, everything being combined into one grand picture and placed in that year because the book was then discovered, with the chronological datum repeated at the close to mark the intention, while Henry explains it by the opposition the work met, so that Josiah could not effect what he designed till his power was thoroughly confirmed, and Ellicott denies that idolatry had been extirpated earlier at all, since Josiah no more than Hezekiah rooted out the spirit of apostasy.
outliers: Henry offers three accounts of how the book came to be missing: carelessly mislaid by those who knew not its value, as some throw their Bibles into a corner; maliciously buried by idolaters restrained from burning it; or carefully hidden by its friends lest it fall into enemy hands.

Ellicott reserves his sharpest reply for a critic's argument that one of the officers named in Chronicles was borrowed from an earlier chapter, as if anything could be inferred from the recurrence of the same name, and that probably in the same family.

11.pericope_label: And it came to pass, when the king had heard the words of the book of the law, that he rent his clothes. And the king commanded Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam the son of Shaphan, and Achbor the son of Michaiah, and Shaphan the scribe, and Asahiah a servant of the king’s, saying, Go ye, enquire of the Lord for me, and for the people, and for all Judah, concerning the words of this book that is found: for great is the wrath of the Lord that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book, to do according unto all that which is written concerning us. So Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam, and Achbor, and Shaphan, and Asahiah, went unto Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe; (now she dwelt in Jerusalem in the college;) and they communed with her. And she said unto them, Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, Tell the man that sent you to me, Thus saith the Lord, Behold, I will bring evil upon this place, and upon the inhabitants thereof, even all the words of the book which the king of Judah hath read: Because they have forsaken me, and have burned incense unto other gods, that they might provoke me to anger with all the works of their hands; therefore my wrath shall be kindled against this place, and shall not be quenched. But to the king of Judah which sent you to enquire of the Lord, thus shall ye say to him, Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, As touching the words which thou hast heard; Because thine heart was tender, and thou hast humbled thyself before the Lord, when thou heardest what I spake against this place, and against the inhabitants thereof, that they should become a desolation and a curse, and hast rent thy clothes, and wept before me; I also have heard thee, saith the Lord. Behold therefore, I will gather thee unto thy fathers, and thou shalt be gathered into thy grave in peace; and thine eyes shall not see all the evil which I will bring upon this place. And they brought the king word again.

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the king's question as asking whether any hope remained for himself and his people or whether the vengeance must fall speedily, and on the phrase written concerning us he notes a conjectural emendation to written therein but prefers the received text, since Josiah identifies the people and their fathers as one nation, while observing that Chronicles reads in this book. On the embassy he supplies the later history of two of its members from the prophet Jeremiah, and takes the king's servant for the officer who attended on the king. The choice of Huldah he explains by residence: why not to Jeremiah or Zephaniah, he asks, and answers that it was apparently because Huldah dwelt in Jerusalem and they did not, at least at this time, Anathoth in Benjamin being Jeremiah's town; she must however have enjoyed a high reputation. Her husband's office he leaves open, either the royal wardrobe or that of the priests' dresses kept in the temple, and in either case holds the man to have been a person of consideration, as the careful specification of his descent further shows. The place where she lived he corrects outright: the rendering college is the Targum's, taken as though the Hebrew word for second were equivalent to the later name of the rabbinic collection, whereas the word really means the second part of the city, that is the lower city. On the oracle he makes three small corrections, that the Hebrew is literally I am about to bring evil, that the versions and Chronicles rightly read upon rather than unto, and that the freedom of expression in the clause about what the king of Judah had read warns us against pressing the earlier words he read it; the works of their hands he glosses as the idols they have made. The word tender he supports from the parallels, and on becoming a desolation and a curse he answers a critic's figure of cause for effect by calling it rather a specification of the type, such as would be made in blessing and cursing. On the last verse he notes the textual variant, that some manuscripts and the old versions give thy grave but the ordinary Hebrew text thy graves may be right, as referring to the burial-place formed by Manasseh, which would contain a number of chambers and niches; and he limits the promise of peace by the words that follow, that his eyes should not see all the evil, so that although Josiah was slain in battle, as the next chapter relates, he was spared the greater calamity of witnessing the ruin of his people. Delitzsch infers from the terms of the commission which passages of the book had been read to the king, namely the curses of the law upon the despisers of the commandments of God, and glosses the phrase for inquiring of the Lord as asking what he has determined. Of the prophetess he says that nothing further is known than what is mentioned here, and that all we can infer from the king's sending to her is that she was highly distinguished on account of her prophetical gifts, and that none of the prophets of renown, such as Jeremiah and Zephaniah, were at that time in Jerusalem. He calls Shallum her father rather than her husband, and takes him for keeper of the clothes, either the priests' dresses kept in the temple or the king's wardrobe, noting that the names of his ancestors are written differently in Chronicles. Her dwelling he places in the second part or district of the city, that is the lower city upon the hill, citing the prophet Zephaniah for the same name. On her reply he marks the exactness of the address: she confirmed the fear Josiah had expressed and proclaimed first the punishments threatened in the book of the law against the rebellious and the idolaters, and then, to the king himself, that on account of his sincere repentance and humiliation he should not live to see the predicted calamities but be gathered to his fathers in peace; the first part of the announcement applies to the man who has sent you to me and the second to the king of Judah who has sent to inquire of the Lord, and though the man who had sent to her was indeed also the king, Delitzsch holds that she intentionally made use of the general term in the first.

Gill draws the plainest inference from the king's grief, that it appears he had never written out a copy of the law as the kings of Israel were ordered to do when they came to the throne, nor had read it, at least not the whole of it; and he finds the fact strange, that a man of twenty-six who had proceeded far in the reformation of worship should be without the book of the law, and the high priest also. It looks, he says, as if it was, as some have thought, that they had till now only some abstracts of the law and not the whole, which is the same explanation Henry reaches independently. The enquiry he supposes directed to some of God's prophets, naming Jeremiah, who had begun to prophesy in the thirteenth year of Josiah's reign and had been a prophet five years. Of Huldah he observes that there had been such prophetesses before, Miriam and Deborah, and then turns to the pagan parallel at some length: in imitation of these, he says, Satan had very early his women prophetesses, the Sibyls, so called from their being the council and oracle of God and consulted as such on occasion, as Huldah now was; he reports from a Byzantine lexicographer that the first of the Sibyls was a Chaldean or a Persian, and some say a Hebrew, from a Greek geographer the express statement that among the Hebrews above Palestine there was a woman prophetess whom some called the Babylonian and others the Egyptian Sibyl, and from a Roman miscellanist that one of them was a Jewess.

Clarke treats the choice of Huldah as the most singular circumstance in the chapter and makes it a standing lesson. At this time Jeremiah was certainly a prophet in Israel, but it is likely he now dwelt at Anathoth and could not readily be consulted; Zephaniah also prophesied under this reign, but probably had not yet begun; Hilkiah was high priest, and the priest's lips should retain knowledge; Shaphan was scribe, and must have been conversant in sacred affairs to be at all fit for his office; and yet Huldah, of whom we know nothing but by this circumstance, is consulted on the meaning of the book of the law, for the secret of the Lord was neither with the high priest nor the scribe nor any other of the servants of the king or ministers of the temple. From this, Clarke says, and we have many facts in all ages to corroborate it, we find that a pontiff or a pope or a bishop or a priest may in some cases not possess the true knowledge of God, and that a simple woman possessing the life of God in her soul may have more knowledge of the divine testimonies than many whose office it is to explain and enforce them; and he adds the judicious remark of another writer, that it pleased God to distinguish several women with the spirit of prophecy as well as other great attainments. The oracle itself he states without softening: the decree is gone forth, Jerusalem shall be delivered into the hands of its enemies, the people will revolt more and more, towards them longsuffering is useless, the wrath of God is kindled and shall not be quenched, and this was a dreadful message. The promise to the king he glosses simply, that because he had feared the Lord and trembled at his word and wept, these evils should not come upon the land in his lifetime. But the words about the grave he takes as a difficulty requiring an answer, since the next chapter relates that Pharaoh-nechoh slew him at Megiddo; and he answers it in two stages. The Assyrians and the Jews were at peace, and Josiah might feel it his duty to oppose the Egyptian king going against his friend and ally and to prevent him from passing through his territories, and in that endeavour he was mortally wounded at Megiddo, but certainly was not killed there, for his servants put him in his second chariot and brought him to Jerusalem, where he died in peace; so that however the place is taken, the words of Huldah were true, since he did die in peace and was gathered to his fathers in peace. Clarke then adds a judgment of his own on the campaign, that from the fuller account we find Josiah should not have meddled in the quarrel between the Egyptian and the Assyrian kings, for God had given a commission to the former against the latter; but he did it in error and suffered for it, and this unfortunate end of a pious man does not at all impeach the credit of the prophetess. Wesley takes the other side of the question about the book's novelty, holding it more probable that Josiah had seen and read it before, but that the great reverence he justly bore to the original book, and the strange and remarkable and seasonable finding of it, had awakened and quickened him to a more serious and diligent consideration of all the passages contained in it; and he exclaims at the providence, that it was still preserved, and that the whole book of God is preserved to us, since if the holy Scriptures had not been of God they had not been in being. The enquiry he glosses as asking what they should do to appease God's wrath, and whether the curses threatened must come upon them without remedy or whether there be hope in Israel concerning the prevention of them. The choice of Huldah he explains by haste and by residence, that the king's earnest affection required great haste and she was in Jerusalem, which is therefore noted in the verse, while Jeremiah might at this time be at Anathoth or in some more remote part of the kingdom, and the like may be said of Zephaniah, who also might not be a prophet at this time though he was afterward. The college he keeps, taking it for the place where the sons of the prophets, or others who devoted themselves to the study of God's word, used to meet and discourse of the things of God and receive the instructions of their teachers. Of her manner he says she uses no compliments: tell the man that sent you, for even kings, though gods to us, are men to God and shall be so dealt with, since with him there is no respect of persons. The tenderness he spells out as trembling at God's word, grief for the dishonour done to God by the sins of his people, and fear of the judgments he saw coming on Jerusalem. And the peace he divides, that it means a time of public peace, for otherwise he died in battle, and that besides he died in peace with God and was by death translated to everlasting peace.

Henry begins by noting what became of the book: we hear no more of the repairing of the temple, but the book found in it occupies us now, and it is not laid up in the king's cabinet as a piece of antiquity, a rarity to be admired, but it is read before the king; those put the truest honour upon their Bibles who study them and converse with them daily, and men of honour and business must look upon an acquaintance with God's word as their best business and honour. The rending of the clothes he reads as the rending of the heart, Josiah being ashamed of the sin of his people and afraid of the wrath of God: he had long thought the case of his kingdom bad by reason of the idolatries found among them, but never thought it so bad as he now perceived it to be. Two things Henry supposes the king wanted to know, what course they should take to turn away God's wrath, since convictions of sin and wrath should put us upon the enquiry what we shall do to be saved, and what they might expect and must provide for; and in the acknowledgement that their fathers had not hearkened to the words of this book he hears a man saying that if this be the rule of right then certainly our fathers have been much in the wrong, and that now the commandment came, sin revived and appeared sin, the law being a glass in which he saw the sins of his people more numerous and more heinous than he had before seen them. On the messengers he observes that by employing those of the first rank the king put an honour upon the oracle. Of the prophetess he says that the spirit of prophecy, that inestimable treasure, was sometimes put not only into earthen vessels but into the weaker vessels, that the excellency of the power might be of God, and he sets Huldah beside Miriam and Deborah, adding that her being a wife was no prejudice at all to her being a prophetess, since marriage is honourable in all. It was a mercy to Jerusalem, he says, that when Bibles were scarce they had prophets, as afterwards, when prophecy ceased, that they had more Bibles, for God never leaves himself without witness because he will leave sinners without excuse. Jeremiah and Zephaniah prophesied at this time, yet the king's messengers made Huldah their oracle, probably because her husband having a place at court they had had more and longer acquaintance with her and greater assurances of her commission than of any other, and had, it is likely, consulted her on other occasions and found that the word of God in her mouth was truth; she was near, dwelling in a place which he takes for the second rank of buildings from the royal palace, and the Jews say she prophesied among the women, the court ladies, being herself one of them. Happy the court, he adds, that had a prophetess within the verge of it and knew how to value her. Her answer he contrasts with a courtier's: she did not send her humble service to his Majesty but spoke in the dialect of a prophetess, from him before whom all stand upon the same level, telling them to carry word to the man that sent them, for even kings, though gods to us, are men to God and shall so be dealt with. The judgment he takes in its degree and duration, a fire so kindled that it shall not be quenched, the decree gone forth and too late to prevent; and in its double reference, to their sins, as if they had designed to provoke him, and to God's own threatenings, since the evil brought is according to the words of the book, so that those who would not be bound by the precept shall be bound by the penalty. The mercy to Josiah he grounds in the tenderness of his heart, and makes much of it: God will distinguish those who distinguish themselves, and where the generality of the people were hardened and their hearts unhumbled, Josiah received the impressions of God's word, trembled at it and yielded to it, and wept before God probably in his closet, but he that sees in secret says it was before him and put every tear of tenderness into his bottle; those who most fear God's wrath are least likely to feel it. He guesses which words had gone to the king's heart, that the land should be brought into desolation, since it was when he heard of the desolation and of the curse that he rent his clothes. The reprieve he reads as a reward reaching beyond this life: Josiah could not prevail to prevent the judgment itself, but God promised that he should not live to see it, which, especially considering that he died in the midst of his days before he was forty, would have been but a small reward for his eminent piety if there had not been another world in which he should be abundantly recompensed. The grave in peace he refers not to the manner of his death, for he was killed in a battle, but to the time of it, a little before the captivity in Babylon, that great trouble in comparison with which the rest were as nothing, so that he might truly be said to die in peace who did not live to share in that; and he died in the love and favour of God, which secures such a peace as no circumstances of dying, not even dying in the field of war, could alter the nature of.

debates: Whether the contents of the book were new to Josiah, where Henry holds that they were new both to the king and to the high priest, since neither the command for the king to write out a copy nor that for the public reading every seventh year can have been long observed, and Gill agrees, inferring that Josiah had never written out a copy nor read the whole and finding it strange that a king of twenty-six should be without the book, with the same explanation of abstracts that Henry reaches; against which Wesley holds it more probable that Josiah had seen and read it before, and that what was new was the force of it, the reverence he bore the original and the seasonable manner of its finding having quickened him to a more diligent consideration of all it contained; while Ellicott warns on textual grounds that the freedom of expression forbids pressing the words he read it as meaning the whole, and Delitzsch says the same of the Hebrew verb.

Why the enquiry went to Huldah rather than to Jeremiah or Zephaniah, where Ellicott and Wesley both answer from residence, that she dwelt in Jerusalem and they did not, Anathoth being Jeremiah's town, Wesley adding the king's haste and the possibility that Zephaniah had not yet begun to prophesy; Henry answers from acquaintance, that her husband's place at court had given them longer knowledge of her and greater assurance of her commission; Delitzsch will infer only that she was highly distinguished and that no prophet of renown was then in the city; and Clarke makes it a standing principle, that the secret of the Lord was with neither the high priest nor the scribe nor any minister of the temple, so that a pontiff or a bishop may not possess the true knowledge of God while a simple woman with the life of God in her soul may know more of the divine testimonies than many whose office it is to explain them.

How the promise of a grave in peace stands with the king's death at Megiddo, where Clarke argues that he was mortally wounded but certainly not killed there, his servants having put him in his second chariot and brought him to Jerusalem where he died in peace, and adds that Josiah should not have meddled in the quarrel at all but did it in error and suffered for it, which does not impeach the prophetess; Henry refers the word not to the manner of his death, for he was killed in a battle, but to its time, a little before the captivity, and to his dying in the love and favour of God; Wesley divides it into a time of public peace and peace with God besides; and Ellicott limits the promise by the clause that follows, that his eyes should not see the evil, so that he was slain in battle but spared the greater calamity.
outliers: Delitzsch calls Shallum the prophetess's father, where the text and every other commentator in the chapter make him her husband; Henry builds on the husband reading, remarking that her being a wife was no prejudice at all to her being a prophetess, since marriage is honourable in all.

Gill sets Huldah beside Miriam and Deborah and then turns to a pagan parallel, that in imitation of such prophetesses Satan had very early his own, the Sibyls, citing a Byzantine lexicographer, a Greek geographer and a Roman miscellanist for the traditions that the first was a Chaldean or a Persian, that one was called the Babylonian or the Egyptian, and that one was a Jewess.
themes: And it came to pass, when the king had heard the words of the book of the law, that he rent his clothes.
And the king commanded Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam the son of Shaphan, and Achbor the son of Michaiah, and Shaphan the scribe, and Asahiah a servant of the king’s, saying,

Go ye, enquire of the Lord for me, and for the people, and for all Judah, concerning the words of this book that is found: for great is the wrath of the Lord that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book, to do according unto all that which is written concerning us.

So Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam, and Achbor, and Shaphan, and Asahiah, went unto Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe; (now she dwelt in Jerusalem in the college;) and they communed with her.
And she said unto them, Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, Tell the man that sent you to me,
Thus saith the Lord, Behold, I will bring evil upon this place, and upon the inhabitants thereof, even all the words of the book which the king of Judah hath read:

Because they have forsaken me, and have burned incense unto other gods, that they might provoke me to anger with all the works of their hands; therefore my wrath shall be kindled against this place, and shall not be quenched.
But to the king of Judah which sent you to enquire of the Lord, thus shall ye say to him, Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, As touching the words which thou hast heard;

Because thine heart was tender, and thou hast humbled thyself before the Lord, when thou heardest what I spake against this place, and against the inhabitants thereof, that they should become a desolation and a curse, and hast rent thy clothes, and wept before me; I also have heard thee, saith the Lord.

Behold therefore, I will gather thee unto thy fathers, and thou shalt be gathered into thy grave in peace; and thine eyes shall not see all the evil which I will bring upon this place. And they brought the king word again.
